content: An anembryonic gestation, also referred to as a blighted ovum, is a type of pregnancy in which an embryo fails to develop within a gestational sac that otherwise appears normal. This condition is thought to result from the early death of the embryo, while the trophoblast (the outer layer of cells that forms part of the placenta) continues to grow. In the early stages, the gestational sac may resemble that of a normal pregnancy, and a yolk sac may even be present. However, a fetal pole, which is the first visible structure of the developing embryo, is absent. This condition is one of the causes of miscarriage. To confirm the diagnosis, the gestational sac must reach a size where the absence of normal embryonic structures can be definitively established. Specifically, an anembryonic pregnancy is diagnosed if a transvaginal ultrasound shows a gestational sac with a mean diameter (MGD) greater than 13 mm without a yolk sac, or a sac with an MGD greater than 18 mm without an embryo. In many clinical settings, a follow-up ultrasound is recommended approximately 10 days after the initial scan to confirm the diagnosis. If the pregnancy has not resulted in a natural miscarriage, several management options are available to address the condition.
